title: Aligned but Apart: Why Cosine Conflict Diagnostics Misread Auxiliary-Loss Interference at the Output Projection
description: Cosine similarity between task gradients is the standard instrument for detecting conflict in multi-task and auxiliary-loss training. At a language model's shared, tied output projection it is misleading. Measuring the per-row gradients that a next-token (CE) and an auxiliary multi-token (MTP) loss deposit there, we find them aligned in direction: on the ~8% of vocabulary rows receiving a target the median per-row cosine is ~0.53 and only ~3-4% are opposed, yet the aggregate cosine over the flattened matrix ranges from near 0 (Muon) to clearly negative (-0.28, AdamW). Per-row gradient norms show both losses loading their magnitude on the same rows (norm-profile cosine 0.98), while 60-69% of that mass sits on a tiny opposed minority (~0.3% of rows, the most frequent function words and punctuation): a norm-weighted cancellation, not disjoint support. An exact rewrite shows the shared-head objective is cross-entropy toward a next-and-future-token mixture, and a zero-parameter estimate of the implied KL cost reproduces 62-91% of the matched within-sweep gap, making the shifted optimum rather than gradient conflict the leading account of the +0.39-nat degradation measured at 124M. Preprint; not peer reviewed. This archive contains the manuscript source, the committed result JSONs every reported number is computed from, the analysis and figure-regeneration scripts, and the claim-verification gate.
